title: Compassion close
hookLine: compassion can grow, with practice and time

cards: A farmer in the state of Song is worried: his grain is coming up too slowly. So he goes out and, one by one, tugs every young stalk upward a little, to help it along.
He comes home worn out and announces he's been helping the crop grow. His son runs out to look. Every plant has withered.
The philosopher Mencius tells this story, and it fits the end of a stretch about something that grows. Today the section on compassion closes, by asking how it grows.

teach.h: A CHILD AT THE EDGE OF A WELL.
teach.b: First, the sprout. Mencius, in the book that carries his name, says anyone who suddenly saw a child about to fall into a well would feel alarm and distress, not for a reward or a reputation, simply because.

In James Legge's translation: "The feeling of commiseration is the principle of benevolence." He calls feelings like this beginnings, small shoots in every person that can grow or wither. Second, the farmer.

teach.h: DON'T NEGLECT IT, DON'T TUG IT.
teach.b: A sprout can be harmed two ways: by neglect, never weeding, or by yanking on it to hurry it. On his telling, goodness grows the way grain grows: tended, daily, without force. Third, the evidence, at its own scale.
The research this path walked through points the same way. Short programs measured gains in compassion. Weeks of loving-kindness moved one measure of bias.
Real changes, modest in size, while some headlines claimed far more, about the vagus nerve and the love hormone.
It grows like grain, not like a magic bean. Fourth, the look back, in this section's lines: warmth, not drowning. Care for carers.
Not in a hurry. Be the one.
For someone else. It spreads. Softer inside.
Modest claims. Not so simple. Pass it on.
Their side. The circle widens. Fierce and kind.
Care heals. Me too. May you be well.
A whole field of sprouts, none of them tugged.

how: In the Confucian tradition, Mencius's "four beginnings" are taught as sprouts of goodness that grow through steady cultivation; some contemplative programs also ask people to keep a simple record of small changes over time.

games.q: in Mencius's story, the farmer of Song thinks his grain is coming up too slowly. what does he do?
o: tug every stalk upward a little, to help it along.
stop weeding, since nothing seems to work.
games.why: he tugs every stalk, comes home proud, and the whole field withers. Mencius warns against both his mistake and its opposite, neglect.

practice: Walk back over the last few weeks and look for one change the size of a sprout: a moment you wished someone well instead of drowning in their trouble, a seat you gave up, a kinder sentence to yourself after a mistake.
Don't tug on it to make it bigger than it was. If nothing comes, that's an honest answer too; it just means keep weeding.

wordCard.voice: Compassion close. The end of this section: compassion as a sprout, grown by tending, slowly, with practice and time. Today's word.

orig.note: Classical Chinese, from the Mencius: the heart of commiseration, one of his four beginnings.

carryVoice: Your line: it grows. Tended, slowly, without force, the way grain grows. And with that, the section closes.
